Family connection
Son in the care of Corva and Veskan Orsival. Corva’s connection was stated at the chancery; legal family registration remains unresolved. The commission records him as Galahad under Collegium sponsorship.
Family record · The Orsivals

Corva and Veskan Orsival. Still married, living separately. Orsival is Veskan’s family name, taken and retained by Corva. Their son died in the hunter strike on the railway; he is the boy Galahad glimpsed in Veskan’s memories.

Corva contains her grief and turns toward practical work and caregiving. Veskan repeatedly returns to the loss, burdened by guilt over a danger he could not have foreseen. Their different ways of grieving drew them apart, while their affection endured.

Corva was Galahad’s principal caregiver; Veskan remained a close paternal presence. His trust in Corva and their enduring bond partly explain why he brought the foundling to her. Galahad regards them both as parents and intends to name Veskan as his father in future family records.

Intended household. Galahad seeks to found and head a noble branch of House Orsival. Both parents would receive matching familial titles: Lady Corva Orsival, Mother of the House, and Sir Veskan Orsival, Father of the House. Their standing recognises parentage. Household duties and delegated authority are assigned separately; neither title confers regency. The household has not been founded and no titles have been granted.

Armament record · Vordrake-bone greatsword

A single long piece of pure white cranial bone forms the blade and integral grip. There is no guard. Its weight makes it difficult for an ordinary man even to lift with two hands; Galahad readily wields it one-handed.

Fashioned from the Vordrake he killed in the wilds, using his hands, nails and abrasion against the remaining skull. Fine inscriptions reproduce protective signs from his reading. Their supernatural effectiveness remains untested.

Rare bone of this quality appears in prestigious local weapons. This blade remains unappraised. Corva and Savel have seen it uncovered. Savel was told that the raw bone came from a trader. The blade is now stored wrapped beneath the bed in Galahad’s Collegium room and carried on private hunts.

Deployment apparatus · Incubation pod

Amniotic medium. Milky nutrient fluid nourishes and cushions the developing body.

Life support. Integrated circulation, filtration and environmental controls sustain the incubation chamber.

Power system. An integrated generator and power-management assembly supply the machinery.

Protective inscriptions. Bile-engineered psychic wards resist hostile Warp influence.

At the last direct observation on Day 0, chamber, life support and integrated power were functional; the amniotic medium had drained and the lid was open. The pod was left in a shattered planting bed beneath the breached glasshouse roof. On Day 8, Veskan reported it unmoved. Superintendent Vardesca ordered it left undisturbed and proposed an inspection. No inspection findings or later operating condition have been recorded.

Origin record

Created by Fabius Bile as an experimental sovereign founder of Homo novus. Principal genetic templates: Fulgrim, Perturabo and Magnus. Selected New Men adaptations and a minor personal contribution from Bile complete the chimeric design.

Primarch-cloning experience and progenoid material taken from Alpha Primus underpin the programme. A period of further experimentation preceded the cohort’s creation.

Transferred from gestation into a deployment pod at approximately one month of age. Accelerated physical maturation is projected over two to five years.

Intended specialisation: psychic technology, combining material engineering with controlled manipulation of the Warp.

Biological assessment

Chimeric physiology

Transhuman strength. Rapid adaptation. An immense psychic potential within a developing body.

Motor and cognitive development

Transhuman strength and speed have enabled an unarmed Vordrake kill and ready one-handed use of its massive bone blade. Enhanced vision and fine motor control support extremely intricate fabrication. A magnifying glass makes tiny work easier but is not necessary for the recorded snake construction. Exceptional recognition of patterns and mechanical relationships complements these physical abilities.

Early station study established fluent speech, independent literacy and practical workshop skills. Collegium study has progressed through all prescribed curricula and two readings of its library. Galahad now researches and occasionally teaches across subjects. Working miniature engines and automata demonstrate his precision; implemented pumping improvements demonstrate applied engineering. Materials, facilities and practical experience still shape what can be realised.

Psychic activity

Psychic potential includes violent force, instinctive defence and receptive telepathy. Emerging receptive sensitivity admits images, emotions, unspoken verbal fragments and associative memory impressions alongside ordinary speech. The subject reports frequent involuntary reception. Corva and Veskan have privately heard his account; some described associations connect with their recollections. Private practice has established controlled small-object movement and brief lifting of a heavy engine assembly. Fine manipulation requires greater concentration than gross lifting. Received impressions can sometimes be reduced in quiet surroundings; crowds, strong emotion and distraction still interfere. Source recognition remains imperfect. Corva has seen occasional small objects shift. Galahad has also presented divination research and reports improvements over the common practices he has tested.

Further practice has developed increasingly targeted emotional influence: comfort and trust, or unease and fear. Some people avoid interrupting him. He can also sustain a calming presence across multiple nearby people while attending to his surroundings; its effect is strongest close to him. Private hunting has established destructive green psychic lightning. Fine sparks now char the edges of his carvings, while forceful discharges produce conspicuous sound, heat and scorched surfaces. Valesse Orchant has witnessed a controlled spark and guides his study of the older arts.

Specialist psychic interference, severe injury and extreme exertion threaten both control and survival.

Stable body and soul

The subject’s own powerful soul is stably integrated with his engineered body. Chronic pain and congenital integration failure are absent.

Physical performance, resilience and cognitive efficiency represent a modest refinement over the Alpha Primus reference. Mature founder capability exceeds that of a standard Custodian while remaining below a true Primarch. Specialities vary across the cohort.

Substantial metabolic reserves support exceptional endurance. An afternoon without food causes no impairment. Prolonged deprivation, extreme exertion, wounds and environmental exposure remain physiological concerns. Control and practical expertise develop with experience.

Toxin resistance

Engineered physiology provides exceptional resistance to most ordinary poisons and venoms. This protection is already active during adolescent development. Common natural toxins are generally neutralised or greatly attenuated; exposures lethal to baseline humans may cause little impairment.

Resistance continues to develop with maturation. Exceptionally potent toxins, very large exposures and specialised agents capable of overcoming transhuman defences can still cause harm. Protection against ordinary toxins does not confer immunity to supernatural corruption. Dose, route of exposure and the agent’s properties determine the outcome.

Observed development

Language and cognition

Exceptional memory and pattern recognition support fluent speech and independent study. Galahad has completed all Collegium curricula and read every book in its library twice, comparing arguments across mathematics, engineering, materials, chemistry, biology, geography, history and economics. He now undertakes resident research and occasional teaching across subjects. Private collections, industrial secrets and other traditions remain further sources. His public accomplishments reveal much more of his aptitude than before; his full capabilities remain concealed.

Receptive psychic impressions are helping associate speech with sensory and emotional meaning. Fragments linked to another person’s recollections can leave useful understanding without a complete remembered scene. Practice has improved the distinction between speech, received fragments and personal interpretation. Their source and accuracy still require judgement.

Fabrication record · Mechanical creations

Clockwork bird. A naturalistic scrap-metal body conceals a wind-up mechanism. Drawing the winding gear down its back stores the energy for short hops and chirruping mechanical sounds.

Articulated snake. More than a hundred thousand tiny components form its mechanism, joints, scales and embellishments. A miniature heat engine drives pistons; contact pressure at the head redirects its movement. A thimbleful of recirculating water is the working fluid, with a separate fuel charge providing heat. It runs for an hour under suitable conditions.

Galahad shaped the parts with fingers and nails, finishing small details against the tip of his supported bone blade. The creations remain in his room alongside miniature engines and research papers.

Monumental architecture. Large halls, towers and elevated galleries exist as structurally sound drawings and calculations. Construction would require substantial funding, industrial capacity and skilled labour.

Craft record · Protective charms

Intricate carvings in teeth, bone, hide and scale taken during private hunts. Interlinked hooked strokes surround a central lozenge; fine emerald sparks darken the borders. These forms derive from local traditions of protection and fortunate passage.

With instruction from Valesse Orchant, some pieces retain faint psychic impressions for hours after attention is withdrawn. Their ability to protect a wearer remains unverified.

Iseva Dorlac has sold forty pieces bearing Galahad’s attribution, retaining one quarter of the receipts. Their public provenance is an exclusive Ceralte supplier.

Psychic engineering · Developmental direction

Material engineering and Warp manipulation form a shared field of aptitude. Potential studies include psychic interaction with mechanisms, responsive materials, interfaces, protective systems and the stabilisation of lasting psychic effects.

Independent experimentation can precede contact with other traditions. Aeldari psychic craftsmanship offers a possible later field of comparative study. Progress depends upon learning, materials and controlled experimentation.

Current record: a substantial research archive, precise mechanical creations and budgeted improvements implemented at the southern pumping works. Faculty engage him as a resident scholar; the chancery has commissioned an examination of the connected delivery system. The earlier small-engine rebuild passed the station’s available load test; the separate long-term housing-life projection remains an estimate. The concealed firearm prototype remains incomplete and unreliable, without a dependable ammunition supply. Charms made under Orchant’s guidance can retain faint psychic impressions for hours, but reliable protective effects and a dependable lasting psychic device have not been demonstrated. No new psychic material has been created.

Homo novus · Founder lineage

The cohort forms an experimental sovereign branch of Homo novus, intended to establish, protect and lead successor populations. Command, research, engineering and guardianship are complementary fields of service.

All founders share Bile-derived ancestry within deliberately diversified genomes. Known harmful shared variants and reproductive incompatibilities have been addressed.

Heritable traits

Reproductive capacity develops after maturity. A founder and a compatible baseline human can produce fertile offspring broadly equivalent to standard New Men. Founder–New Men pairings produce New Men with possible individual adaptations.

Compatible founders may also reproduce. Heritable population traits are engineered separately from the complete founder phenotype; inheritance of the full proto-Primarch design is not assured.

New Men populations reproduce independently across subsequent generations.

Temperamental profile

Investigative curiosity, analytical confidence, an appetite for control and a drive to improve and redesign. Fulgrim-derived refinement, Perturabo-derived constructive logic, Magnus-derived psychic curiosity and Bile-derived adaptive ambition inform the subject’s disposition.

Potential tendencies include ruthlessness, superiority, possessiveness and an instrumental view of others. Experience and personal judgement shape their expression.

In private discussion with Corva, Galahad has advocated one government for eastern Vesalius and prioritised victory and survival over conventional moral judgement. His stated goal is enduring safety and stability for his people, with a future extending into the stars.

I

Otranto

Fortified terraces, agricultural basins and mountain railways. Foundries support courtly wealth; water and transport shape political power.

II

Morholt

Glacial mountains, immense conifers and coal-heated fortress cities. Supply trains connect generating stations and mines; old ruins contain decayed conventional machinery.

III

Vesalius

Volcanic uplands, jungle and violent seas. Armoured cargo vessels connect fortified harbours beneath bronze navigation beacons.

The preserve

Technologically superior xenos hunt dangerous wildlife and humans. Their surveillance is imperfect, their visits intermittent. Attempts to challenge their access to the world invite retaliation.

The hunters range across Malaspina and nearby systems. Their reach dwarfs every local human power.

Industry & the empyrean

Human industry produces conventional firearms, artillery, tanks, propeller aircraft, electrical grids and radio. Rare captured hunter devices function in local hands, guarded by the few who understand their operation. Secluded traditions study magic, warding and the older arts; some experiment with effects upon machinery.

Isolation record

A Dark Age of Technology colony cut off during the Age of Strife, never incorporated into the Imperium. Local civilisation rebuilt after collapse; Imperial institutions and recognisable teachings are absent. Ancient human offworld fragments are exceptionally rare, broken and effectively unrecognisable.

Captured hunter technology

Rare captured hunter weapons and devices circulate as guarded trophies, military assets and objects of study. Earlier generations of human soldiers and scholars have already learned to operate some examples and partially understand a few systems. Limited repairs, adaptations and cannibalisation are possible where knowledge and parts survive; reliable manufacture of their advanced cores, power sources and specialised components is beyond the current industrial base.

A world denied progress

Malaspina is held in enforced technological stagnation. Human ingenuity produces advances, but recurrent hunter attacks destroy workshops, infrastructure, records and skilled communities, while recovery operations reclaim or destroy captured equipment. Concentrated alien arsenals, conspicuous use and threatening research attract particular attention. Losses repeatedly offset gains; permanent war preparations and death-world maintenance consume the resources needed for sustained development. Even without the hunters, survival would demand substantial labour. Raids are intermittent locally, but their cumulative pressure is planetary and persistent. Imperfect surveillance permits concealed caches and scattered expertise to survive.

Local record

Serravonne

A fortified secondary port and railway junction in the March of Veyrasse on eastern Vesalius, reached by the hillside railway. Cleared ground, drainage works and guarded rail access protect its industrial yards. Dark stone and concrete walls overlook crowded roofs, chimneys and harbour lights.

The station contains a maintenance room with benches, work clothing, a stove, a ledger desk and a wall telephone. Galahad lived under Corva’s care from his first night until leaving for Auvrienne, sleeping in an alcove adjoining the kitchen. It remains his family home; his current lodging is at the Collegium. Superintendent Leont Vardesca has authorised his meals and necessary clothing on the station account. A storeroom, washroom and workshop support the station’s daily work. The alcove bed has been lengthened as Galahad grows. During the year, a hunter strike on a pumping installation farther along the line disrupted deliveries and made emergency repairs the workshop’s priority.

Local record

Auvrienne

Auvrienne, Veyrasse’s capital, rises in terraces above an extensive railway basin. Freight warehouses, cranes and furnace-lit workshops occupy the lower city. Retaining walls support roads climbing toward pale government buildings with steep roofs and narrow towers. Gun positions overlook the railway cutting. Electric trams serve the streets. Near the freight-yard exit stand a booking office and a glass-covered street plan; farther uphill are an iron-railed monument and an illuminated inn. A bookseller occupies a nearer shopfront.

The Auvrienne Collegium of Civil Engineering occupies a broad terrace behind iron railings, with a grey-stone main building, courtyard and teaching workshops. Odran Savel serves as Examiner in Mechanics and sponsors Galahad’s work. Following completion of all curricula, Galahad remains a resident scholar and occasional teacher, receiving a stipend alongside lodging and meals. The library has been read twice; specialised collections and laboratories retain separate access arrangements. Institutional and professional connections support his expanding research.

The Margrave resides and governs in a fortified palace and government precinct on Auvrienne’s upper terraces, overlooking the city and railway basin. The household occupies the palace; adjoining buildings contain the chancery, treasury and military secretariat. Court and state policy are centred there, while municipal offices administer the city. The Collegium maintains connections through engineering work and patronage.

Bestiary · Vordrake

The Vordrake, also called the furnace drake, is a house-sized winged reptile capable of breathing flame. Folded wings lie along its flanks in overlapping seams; ridged throat folds hang below a wedge-shaped head, with pale mineral growths along the jaw. Its exceptionally dense white cranial bone is known from natural histories and prized for rare weapons. Hunting accounts describe organised armed parties and substantial ammunition expenditure. Bringing one down barehanded lies beyond ordinary local expectations.

Regional political and military archive

Eastern Vesalius

Serravonne lies within the March of Veyrasse. No continent is unified; defended settlements and transport corridors determine the reach of government.

Political geography

None of Malaspina’s three principal continents is unified. States hold defended settlements, cultivated districts and the transport corridors between them; large areas within their claimed borders remain beyond effective control. Hereditary claims, municipal privileges and commercial obligations frequently overlap.

Otranto contains the largest territorial powers and strongest mass armies. Morholt favours fortress leagues and dispersed forces adapted to forest and mountain terrain. Vesalius places greater weight on ports, coastal shipping and securing narrow routes inland. Overseas possessions and treaty ports are possible, but sustaining a large transcontinental empire would be exceptionally difficult.

The powers surrounding Serravonne form one regional political neighbourhood, not an exhaustive division of Vesalius or the planet.

March of Veyrasse

Veyrasse occupies part of Vesalius’s eastern coast: several fortified ports, cultivated coastal valleys and inland mining districts connected by railway. Serravonne is a secondary port and railway junction, strategically valuable but distant from the seat of government.

A hereditary margrave rules through a charter negotiated with landed houses, municipal councils and industrial proprietors. The margrave commands the standing army and conducts foreign relations. The other institutions supply much of the money, transport and manpower, giving them considerable influence over policy and mobilisation.

Engineers receive substantial professional respect, while education and patronage offer opportunities accompanied by obligations. Workshops, land and schooling are shaped by the interests of their patrons. Railway superintendent Leont Vardesca exercises authority over railway affairs and dependants; his office does not confer command of Serravonne’s government or army.

Duchy of Caldrienne

North of Veyrasse along the coast, Caldrienne is a more centralised hereditary state with productive agricultural valleys and substantial armaments works. Its army combines disciplined infantry, strong field artillery and the region’s greatest concentration of tanks.

Caldrienne is Veyrasse’s principal territorial rival. An armed truce restrains their dispute over the Cressault corridor, while trade continues across the frontier.

Karsenne Compact

Inland beyond the coastal escarpment, Karsenne is a federation of mining towns and fortress districts whose councils jealously protect their autonomy. Its military strengths are mountain troops, engineers, demolition specialists and fortified passes.

Karsenne is an essential supplier and uneasy defensive partner of Veyrasse. Its councils resent dependence on Veyrasse’s coastal export routes and are disputing freight charges. They seek an alternative route through Calvernis; Veyrasse regards that project as a threat to its revenues and strategic influence.

Calvernis Republic

South along the coast, Calvernis is governed through a restricted franchise dominated by competing shipping, banking and industrial families. Its military strengths include convoy escorts, coastal artillery, marines and propeller-driven maritime aircraft.

Calvernis is both a major commercial partner and a rival of Veyrasse, competing for railway contracts, harbour business and influence in smaller settlements. Its potential alternative export route for Karsenne adds to these tensions.

Ceralte Admiralty

Ceralte occupies an offshore island chain. A hereditary protector shares power with a council of senior naval officers and island governors. Experienced crews, torpedo craft, minelaying and operations in difficult coastal waters are its principal military strengths.

Ceralte is a treaty partner against piracy and hunter incursions. Mainland interests frequently accuse it of sheltering privateers targeting their commerce; accusation alone does not establish official complicity.

Trade and dependence

None of the regional powers can afford complete economic independence. Caldrienne purchases ores from Karsenne; Karsenne needs coastal ports; Veyrasse purchases machinery and shipping services from Calvernis; Ceralte imports grain. Political enemies remain customers and suppliers.

Disputes over Karsenne’s freight charges and alternative export route could end in negotiation, economic confrontation or armed conflict. No outcome has been settled.

Cressault corridor

The Cressault corridor is a chain of defended valleys near the Veyrasse–Caldrienne frontier, containing a railway crossing, irrigated farmland and the pumping infrastructure sustaining them. Both states claim it. Some estates owe hereditary obligations to one government while depending on the other for transport and protection.

A previous border war ended in an armistice without resolving ownership. Frontier troops exchange occasional fire and patrols sometimes fail to return. Customs inspections and railway delays serve as instruments of pressure. Both governments accuse the other of supporting armed local claimants and interfering with water supplies.

Renewed war is feared, but neither government has publicly committed to it. Serravonne is away from this front; its railway carries associated supplies and returning personnel.

Service and internal tensions

Conscription and industrial obligations create friction within Veyrasse. Wealthier households can secure favourable postings and protected occupations for their dependants. Poorer districts supply a disproportionate share of dangerous perimeter and field service.

Railway workers possess bargaining power because transport stoppages threaten both military operations and food deliveries. The station’s stores, schedules and workshops form part of the wider military economy. Staff maintaining civilian machinery also support military transport and defensive installations.

Veyrasse military institutions

The standing army fields infantry, artillery, engineers, a limited armoured force and supporting services. It fights other states and reinforces threatened districts.

Territorial garrisons combine local reservists with permanent cadres responsible for walls, alarms, evacuation routes, magazines and perimeter patrols.

Household forces belong to major estates and industrial patrons. Charters define their obligations to the state, but personal loyalties often remain strongest.

Serravonne defences

Serravonne maintains a permanent garrison, coastal gun positions, a mobilisation depot and railway-security personnel. Surrounding districts keep reserve rolls and emergency stores. Military engineers work on bridges, drainage systems and defensive clearings.

These institutions coexist with civilian railway administration. Control of transport, stores, military units and municipal affairs is divided rather than concentrated in the superintendent’s office.

Defence against the hunters

Against other human states, armies can pursue military victory and territorial settlements. Against hunter incursions, defenders commonly prioritise preserving communications, evacuating exposed people, denying easy approaches and concentrating conventional fire when an attacker becomes vulnerable.

Fortifications offer shelter and fighting positions, but cannot guarantee protection against attacks from above. Killing an isolated hunter is one form of success; preserving a reservoir or substantially reducing casualties can be another.

Warning agreements and limited mutual assistance connect rival states. Governments still dispute whether intervention will preserve a useful buffer, exhaust their reserves or expose their own forces to attack. Their shared enemy has not abolished competition.

Confirmed collaboration with hunters is rare and must be distinguished from widespread allegations. A settlement’s survival, a returning expedition or possession of a captured device may provoke suspicion without establishing collaboration.

Family, standing and service

Women and men may head noble houses, hold property and inherit rank on equal terms under the governing grant. Mother and Father of the House are matching familial titles recognising parentage; household responsibilities are delegated separately and neither title confers regency.

The Margrave can create minor hereditary noble houses by formal grant within Veyrasse’s charter. Grants define the recognised branch and succession. Land, military privileges and political seats require separate provision; ownership of an estate alone does not confer nobility.

Veyrasse distinguishes noble houses, named common families and those without a recognised surname. Family records shape access and assumptions about worth. Education, patronage and useful service offer routes into circles that remain acutely conscious of lineage.

The chancery occupies the palace’s eastern approach, linked to neighbouring offices by a roofed gallery. Portraits, family distinctions and dark green leather furnish its waiting rooms. Its works-expenditure office commissions technical reports and examines requests for public funds.

Local accounts use lorrats, each divided into one hundred brins. A skilled worker may earn roughly twenty-five lorrats a month.

Galahad’s regional knowledge

Through the first year’s books, railway conversation and local news, Galahad has learned the broad regional political geography, the states’ military specialisations and relationships, the Cressault dispute, and the significance of freight, food and mobilisation. His private research now includes military and economic projections for regional unification, discussed with Corva at the station.

Planetary reference

Continents, powers and the older arts

Approximately 1.21 billion inhabitants across three divided continents.

Planetary population survey

Malaspina supports approximately 1.21 billion people. Regional estimates total 1,209.2 million: Otranto 757.0 million, Vesalius 340.4 million and Morholt 111.8 million. Registers are uneven, borders disputed and wilderness settlements difficult to count. These figures describe inhabitants rather than mobilisable armies. The five eastern Vesalian states together account for 68.6 million people under separate governments. Veyrasse's 15.7 million occupy a claimed area of roughly 237,000 square kilometres, with settlement concentrated in defended districts.

Otranto: crowns, republics and disputed authority

Veldrassen is an old composite monarchy whose provincial bargains constrain taxation and mobilisation. Its large industrial base supports foundries, railways, arsenals and diversified manufacturing. Ostrevain is a centralising monarchy extending tighter administration across an extensive agricultural hinterland and expanding modern arsenals. Their governments command substantial resources but must bargain with institutions within their own territories.

Rovessara is a coastal commercial republic with strong precision, electrical, optical and aircraft-engine industries alongside a diversified economy. Its financiers and merchants hold interests overseas. Brannervaux is a river federation of unequal cities and estates, negotiating water allocation and taxation; agricultural processing, chemistry and major waterworks sustain its economy. Cervaud is a militarised border duchy under competing larger patrons' influence. Veylac is a smaller industrial republic with unresolved frontier disputes.

Ossavren's former crownlands contain rival claimants, provincial armies and ports administering separate customs. Veldrassen and Ostrevain support different contenders. The old crown's population and industry remain divided among authorities; no single palace commands them all. Smaller states, clients and autonomous territories fill the remaining political landscape. Annexation, foreign concessions and limited sovereignty are established realities.

Morholt: valleys, concessions and fortress jurisdictions

Rovengard is the largest single monarchy, centred on settled southern valleys with scattered forest and mountain strongholds. Varnesk is a mining and industrial league in which councils and foundry interests negotiate control; specialist steels, bearings and durable machinery are important trades. Galdresk's wardenship combines chartered orders, estates and civilian institutions, with expertise in field medicine and communications and small houses preserving the older arts. Halskert is a river republic whose seasonal shipping and agricultural valleys sustain influential dock and mill proprietors.

Beyond these governments lie numerous fortress jurisdictions, dependent districts and settlements. Some mineral and railway concessions are financed by Otrantan interests while local authorities retain civil government. Food, heating and seasonal transport constrain military operations. Great forest claims encompass little dependable tax revenue or manpower; control follows defended valleys and supply routes.

Vesalius beyond the eastern chart

Tervayne is a western maritime power separated from Veyrasse by roughly two thousand kilometres of uplands, forests and intervening jurisdictions. There is no continuous transcontinental railway. Its shipping interests compete with Calvernis overseas; its army is not stationed at Veyrasse's frontier.

Vardol lies farther north beyond Caldrienne's northern approaches. It rivals the inland realm of Averholt, whose populated basins and provincial arrangements shape its government. Their contested frontier and internal obligations consume resources that cannot simply be directed toward annexing the eastern coast.

Serevask's disputed federation collectively contains 58.4 million inhabitants, but the federal seat effectively administers only 13 million. Varnelle's delta authorities control commercial customs and their own troops; Kelbrun's upriver councils and plantation interests maintain separate levies; Gavrel's chartered march houses retain armed forces. Disputes over debt, water and federal authority have produced recurring internal conflict. Southern workshops preserve experience in rubber chemistry, filtration and medicine across these divided jurisdictions.

Elsewhere stand smaller states, independent ports and commercial territories. Veyrasse's security depends on its own army and revenues, difficult inland approaches, conditional partnerships and other powers' competing interests. Karsenne guards its passes; Calvernis resists a single power monopolising coastal commerce; Ceralte's maritime partnerships matter. Rivalries remain real, coalitions uncertain and defeat possible. Hunter attacks burden all governments without guaranteeing any border.

Industry and the circulation of knowledge

Industrial capability varies between districts as well as countries. The leading centres possess mature steelworking, aluminium production, casting, welding, machine tools, electrical networks, industrial chemistry and combustion engines. Conventional land armies, propeller aircraft and steam or diesel shipping depend on fuel, skilled labour and reliable maintenance. Experimental radio detection remains a developing field. Older machinery continues in widespread service alongside the most modern local equipment.

Regional concentrations of expertise arise from institutions, resources, trade and accumulated practice. Large states possess diversified economies; a famous precision workshop does not make its country the sole source of precision work. New designs may exceed current practice, while reproducible manufacture and large-scale adoption present their own demands.

Institutions of the older arts

Reliable practitioners are exceptionally rare, but accumulated records are much more extensive. Historians, physicians, scribes and instrument makers sustain schools whose few gifted members may travel between patrons. A teaching house can preserve generations of observations without producing an exceptional pupil in every generation.

Veldrassen maintains court examination offices and provincial registries. Rovessaran institutes and hospitals collect documented cases; Brannervaux's estates preserve private archives. Small teaching houses accompany Galdresk's wardens, while guarded Varnesk workshops occasionally collaborate with practitioners. Ceralte has maritime traditions, and Vesalian ports carry itinerant teachers and texts alongside private circles such as those in Auvrienne.

Scholarly, hereditary and religious schools dispute method and interpretation within each society. Divination, warding, telekinesis, ritual binding and rare experiments with machinery remain living pursuits. Ordinary study can preserve and interpret knowledge without granting every student the ability to perform it. The Collegium's limited regard for these subjects is a local academic attitude. Orchant's instruction and Galahad's observed lingering charm impressions remain part of this wider tradition; dependable protective effects remain unproven.

Open the complete world record

Malaspina is an isolated human death world of ancient industrial cities, fortified aristocratic estates, and immense wildernesses. Its inhabitants live beneath the recurring threat of technologically superior xenos who use the planet as a hunting preserve. Human civilisation endures through heavy industry, disciplined military service, locally maintained technology, and jealously guarded traditions of psychic practice.

Founded by human settlers during the Dark Age of Technology, Malaspina lost interstellar contact during the Age of Strife. It was never brought into Imperial Compliance and has no surviving Imperial administration, Mechanicus establishment, Ecclesiarchy or recognisable Imperial creed. Its founding civilisation collapsed through isolation and repeated local catastrophes; present societies rebuilt unevenly from the remains.

Three principal continents divide its inhabited surface: Otranto, Morholt, and Vesalius. Each supports distinct human societies shaped by its terrain, resources, and exposure to the hunters. No government commands the entire planet or any of its three principal continents. Authority belongs to competing city-states, hereditary houses, military strongholds, and industrial oligarchies whose territories overlap through treaties, marriages, debts, and longstanding claims.

Otranto holds the greatest concentration of population and industry. Jagged mountain chains enclose broad agricultural basins, while rivers connect densely settled valleys. Its cities climb fortified terraces: ivory palaces and copper domes overlook manufactoria, workers’ districts, rail terminals, and smoking foundries. Monumental aqueducts cross crowded avenues. Armoured trains pass through mountain tunnels and over immense viaducts, carrying grain, ore, troops, and machinery between defended settlements.

Otranto’s cultivated districts depend upon extensive drainage works, pumping stations, reservoirs, and maintained perimeter defences. Beyond these enclosures, forests advance rapidly across cleared ground. Agricultural wealth confers considerable political power, and disputes over water, transport routes, and food exports are frequent causes of conflict.

Morholt is colder, more heavily forested, and more sparsely settled. Towering conifers cover deep valleys beneath glacial mountains. Snowbound fortress cities surround coal-fired generating stations, district-heating plants, mineral workings, and sheltered industrial sites. Heated glasshouses provide food within their walls. Tracked vehicles and armoured supply trains connect the larger settlements, while distant outposts depend on seasonal expeditions.

The wilderness of Morholt contains extensive remnants of earlier human occupation. Marble colonnades stand among enormous roots; collapsed transit lines disappear beneath ferns and luminous fungi. Some ruins contain corroded boilers, seized pumps and collapsed industrial workings from earlier local settlements. Any surviving fragments of the original interstellar colony are exceptionally rare, broken and effectively unrecognisable. Others have become dens for native predators or sites frequented by the alien hunters. Local troops specialise in reconnaissance, tracking, survival, and combat beneath the forest canopy.

Vesalius is a continent of volcanic uplands, dense jungles, and violent coastal weather. Steaming rivers descend through black basalt terraces. Offshore stone pillars and rugged cliffs shelter deep natural harbours. Human settlement concentrates along the coasts, where fortified ports support shipyards, fisheries, mineral exports, and maritime trade.

Vesalian cities rise in crowded terraces above their waterfronts. Copper roofs, stone mansions, furnace chimneys, and bronze navigation beacons overlook drydocks and armoured cargo vessels. Inland, flowering vegetation covers abandoned airfields, overgrown terraces and the weathered foundations of forgotten settlements. Expeditions seek mineral deposits and recoverable conventional machinery, supported by small settlements whose survival depends on regular coastal supply.

Malaspina’s ecology makes permanent habitation an undertaking requiring constant labour. Large predators stalk livestock, patrols, and industrial clearings. Some possess heavy natural plating; others hunt through heightened sensitivity to vibration, heat, or scent. Seasonal fungal blooms threaten stored food and exposed lungs. Aggressive vegetation invades roads, drainage channels, and foundations. Waterborne parasites require reliable treatment and filtration.

These hazards sustain entire professions. Perimeter crews clear vegetation, military engineers maintain transport corridors, and specialist workers inspect filters, reservoirs, and food stores. A settlement’s security depends as much on functioning machinery and dependable supplies as on its weapons.

Human culture combines elaborate courtly traditions with industrial militarism. Noble households maintain formal uniforms, heraldic devices, genealogical records, and private military forces. Officers wear high collars, long coats, polished armour, and carefully displayed service distinctions. Ivory, deep green, bronze, and gold feature prominently among Otranto’s wealthy households, while regional forces adopt clothing suited to their environments.

Prestige also belongs to skilled artificers, engineers, physicians, and scholars. Patronage of a foundry, academy, hospital, or public conservatory demonstrates wealth and authority. Art, music, ornamental craftsmanship, and monumental architecture flourish wherever resources permit. Beneath that splendour, much of the population works in demanding conditions, bound to employers and ruling families through inherited obligations, debt, or dependence upon protected accommodation.

Human technology is unevenly distributed, concentrated in defended industrial centres and their military arsenals. Factories produce steel, machine tools, electrical equipment, industrial chemicals, combustion engines and conventional armoured vehicles. Coal and oil power thermal stations, while suitable regions exploit hydroelectricity. Wired telephones, telegraph networks and radio support communications.

A wealthy household can equip its retainers with well-made rifles, submachine guns, machine guns, mortars and artillery, supported by tanks, armoured cars and military trucks. Poorer provincial levies rely on older firearms and limited ammunition. Propeller-driven aircraft operate from defended airfields, and steel steamships and diesel vessels serve the coasts. Access to fuel, replacement components, trained personnel and transport determines military strength. Native humanity has no working spacecraft or orbital infrastructure. Exceptionally rare ancient human offworld debris is broken and effectively unrecognisable.

Rare captured hunter weapons and devices circulate as guarded trophies, military assets and objects of study. Earlier generations of human soldiers and scholars have already learned to operate some examples and partially understand a few systems. Limited repairs, adaptations and cannibalisation are possible where knowledge and parts survive; reliable manufacture of their advanced cores, power sources and specialised components is beyond the current industrial base.

Magic and the older arts are recognised features of life. Their interpretation varies between societies; local traditions describe psychic phenomena through their own vocabulary and inherited practices. Some communities place psykers under religious supervision; others employ them through scholarly institutions, hereditary service, or secretive circles of practitioners. Divination, warding, telekinesis, and ritual binding are studied with differing degrees of understanding and success.

Experiments combining machinery and psychic effects exist, usually within heavily guarded workshops or secluded sanctuaries. Such devices remain rare, temperamental, and dependent on particular practitioners. Records are fragmented, discoveries are closely guarded, and rival traditions frequently disagree over the causes of their successes and failures. Psychic practice offers real capabilities while carrying the dangers inherent in contact with the Warp.

The hunters are a regional spacefaring xenos species whose reach encompasses Malaspina and nearby systems. Their dominion is overwhelmingly vast to local human societies.

The alien hunters operate across all three continents. They arrive from offworld in advanced craft. Masked humanoid trophy-hunters employ sophisticated armour, active concealment, sensors and pulse weaponry. Their expeditions target dangerous wildlife as well as humans. Decorated soldiers, experienced wilderness fighters, and powerful psykers can attract particular attention.

The humans experience their presence as a continuing war punctuated by raids, disappearances, ambushes, and destructive interventions. The hunters treat human resistance as part of the preserve’s value. Their activity varies between expeditions: some pursue individual prey, others attack military formations or interfere with particular installations.

They maintain sites in remote regions and respond aggressively to developments that threaten their access to the planet. Attempts to follow their craft with optical observation or experimental radio detection, approach their remote sites, or organise sustained attacks against their facilities have drawn retaliation. They would resist a future challenge to their offworld access; native humans have no established orbital programme. Their presence is intermittent and their surveillance imperfect, allowing human societies considerable freedom within a wider condition of confinement.

Malaspina is held in enforced technological stagnation. Human ingenuity produces advances, but recurrent hunter attacks destroy workshops, infrastructure, records and skilled communities, while recovery operations reclaim or destroy captured equipment. Concentrated alien arsenals, conspicuous use and threatening research attract particular attention. Losses repeatedly offset gains; permanent war preparations and death-world maintenance consume the resources needed for sustained development. Even without the hunters, survival would demand substantial labour. Raids are intermittent locally, but their cumulative pressure is planetary and persistent. Imperfect surveillance permits concealed caches and scattered expertise to survive.

The shared threat has produced alliances, mutual defence arrangements, and exchanges of military knowledge. It has also encouraged secrecy, appeasement, and accusations of collaboration. Rival states continue to compete for resources and territory, each convinced that control of its own institutions is essential to survival.

Malaspina remains a divided, inhabited world with substantial industrial resources, established cultures, decayed ruins, and vast territories beyond reliable human control. Its cities preserve wealth and learning behind formidable defences, while the wilderness and the skies remain contested.

Political geography. None of Malaspina’s three principal continents is unified. States hold defended settlements, cultivated districts and the transport corridors between them; large areas within their claimed borders remain beyond effective control. Hereditary claims, municipal privileges and commercial obligations frequently overlap.

Otranto contains the largest territorial powers and strongest mass armies. Morholt favours fortress leagues and dispersed forces adapted to forest and mountain terrain. Vesalius places greater weight on ports, coastal shipping and securing narrow routes inland. Overseas possessions and treaty ports are possible, but sustaining a large transcontinental empire would be exceptionally difficult.

The powers surrounding Serravonne form one regional political neighbourhood, not an exhaustive division of Vesalius or the planet.

March of Veyrasse. Veyrasse occupies part of Vesalius’s eastern coast: several fortified ports, cultivated coastal valleys and inland mining districts connected by railway. Serravonne is a secondary port and railway junction, strategically valuable but distant from the seat of government.

A hereditary margrave rules through a charter negotiated with landed houses, municipal councils and industrial proprietors. The margrave commands the standing army and conducts foreign relations. The other institutions supply much of the money, transport and manpower, giving them considerable influence over policy and mobilisation.

Engineers receive substantial professional respect, while education and patronage offer opportunities accompanied by obligations. Workshops, land and schooling are shaped by the interests of their patrons. Railway superintendent Leont Vardesca exercises authority over railway affairs and dependants; his office does not confer command of Serravonne’s government or army.

Duchy of Caldrienne. North of Veyrasse along the coast, Caldrienne is a more centralised hereditary state with productive agricultural valleys and substantial armaments works. Its army combines disciplined infantry, strong field artillery and the region’s greatest concentration of tanks.

Caldrienne is Veyrasse’s principal territorial rival. An armed truce restrains their dispute over the Cressault corridor, while trade continues across the frontier.

Karsenne Compact. Inland beyond the coastal escarpment, Karsenne is a federation of mining towns and fortress districts whose councils jealously protect their autonomy. Its military strengths are mountain troops, engineers, demolition specialists and fortified passes.

Karsenne is an essential supplier and uneasy defensive partner of Veyrasse. Its councils resent dependence on Veyrasse’s coastal export routes and are disputing freight charges. They seek an alternative route through Calvernis; Veyrasse regards that project as a threat to its revenues and strategic influence.

Calvernis Republic. South along the coast, Calvernis is governed through a restricted franchise dominated by competing shipping, banking and industrial families. Its military strengths include convoy escorts, coastal artillery, marines and propeller-driven maritime aircraft.

Calvernis is both a major commercial partner and a rival of Veyrasse, competing for railway contracts, harbour business and influence in smaller settlements. Its potential alternative export route for Karsenne adds to these tensions.

Ceralte Admiralty. Ceralte occupies an offshore island chain. A hereditary protector shares power with a council of senior naval officers and island governors. Experienced crews, torpedo craft, minelaying and operations in difficult coastal waters are its principal military strengths.

Ceralte is a treaty partner against piracy and hunter incursions. Mainland interests frequently accuse it of sheltering privateers targeting their commerce; accusation alone does not establish official complicity.

Trade and dependence. None of the regional powers can afford complete economic independence. Caldrienne purchases ores from Karsenne; Karsenne needs coastal ports; Veyrasse purchases machinery and shipping services from Calvernis; Ceralte imports grain. Political enemies remain customers and suppliers.

Disputes over Karsenne’s freight charges and alternative export route could end in negotiation, economic confrontation or armed conflict. No outcome has been settled.

Cressault corridor. The Cressault corridor is a chain of defended valleys near the Veyrasse–Caldrienne frontier, containing a railway crossing, irrigated farmland and the pumping infrastructure sustaining them. Both states claim it. Some estates owe hereditary obligations to one government while depending on the other for transport and protection.

A previous border war ended in an armistice without resolving ownership. Frontier troops exchange occasional fire and patrols sometimes fail to return. Customs inspections and railway delays serve as instruments of pressure. Both governments accuse the other of supporting armed local claimants and interfering with water supplies.

Renewed war is feared, but neither government has publicly committed to it. Serravonne is away from this front; its railway carries associated supplies and returning personnel.

Service and internal tensions. Conscription and industrial obligations create friction within Veyrasse. Wealthier households can secure favourable postings and protected occupations for their dependants. Poorer districts supply a disproportionate share of dangerous perimeter and field service.

Railway workers possess bargaining power because transport stoppages threaten both military operations and food deliveries. The station’s stores, schedules and workshops form part of the wider military economy. Staff maintaining civilian machinery also support military transport and defensive installations.

Veyrasse military institutions. The standing army fields infantry, artillery, engineers, a limited armoured force and supporting services. It fights other states and reinforces threatened districts.

Territorial garrisons combine local reservists with permanent cadres responsible for walls, alarms, evacuation routes, magazines and perimeter patrols.

Household forces belong to major estates and industrial patrons. Charters define their obligations to the state, but personal loyalties often remain strongest.

Serravonne defences. Serravonne maintains a permanent garrison, coastal gun positions, a mobilisation depot and railway-security personnel. Surrounding districts keep reserve rolls and emergency stores. Military engineers work on bridges, drainage systems and defensive clearings.

These institutions coexist with civilian railway administration. Control of transport, stores, military units and municipal affairs is divided rather than concentrated in the superintendent’s office.

Defence against the hunters. Against other human states, armies can pursue military victory and territorial settlements. Against hunter incursions, defenders commonly prioritise preserving communications, evacuating exposed people, denying easy approaches and concentrating conventional fire when an attacker becomes vulnerable.

Fortifications offer shelter and fighting positions, but cannot guarantee protection against attacks from above. Killing an isolated hunter is one form of success; preserving a reservoir or substantially reducing casualties can be another.

Warning agreements and limited mutual assistance connect rival states. Governments still dispute whether intervention will preserve a useful buffer, exhaust their reserves or expose their own forces to attack. Their shared enemy has not abolished competition.

Confirmed collaboration with hunters is rare and must be distinguished from widespread allegations. A settlement’s survival, a returning expedition or possession of a captured device may provoke suspicion without establishing collaboration.

Galahad’s regional knowledge. Through the first year’s books, railway conversation and local news, Galahad has learned the broad regional political geography, the states’ military specialisations and relationships, the Cressault dispute, and the significance of freight, food and mobilisation. This is contextual knowledge of the society around him.

Regional survey II. The eastern Vesalian atlas covers a region approximately 1,200 km east–west by 1,600 km north–south. Its local grid uses kilometres. Territorial shading records claims rather than continuous occupation. Caldrienne extends beyond the northern edge and Calvernis beyond the southern edge; their mapped areas are portions of larger states.

Veyrasse spans approximately 715 km north–south and up to 440 km east–west, with a charted claim of about 237,000 km². Karsenne’s charted claim covers about 263,000 km² across an elongated escarpment region about 1,000 km north–south. The Ceralte island chain shown spans about 915 km north–south and contains roughly 39,000 km² of charted island land; the intervening sea is not counted as land area. The disputed Cressault belt contains approximately 15,000 km² of overlapping claims and must not be counted as an additional sovereign state.

Auvrienne is Veyrasse’s seat of government, north of Serravonne. Valdrec is Caldrienne’s capital; Drossane hosts Karsenne’s councils; Miravelle is Calvernis’s government centre; Dalmor is Ceralte’s naval administrative seat on its principal central island. Serravonne remains a secondary fortified port and railway junction. The Ressant descends from the escarpment toward the Serravonne harbour area.

The main railway connects Serravonne northward to Auvrienne and the Cressault crossing, continuing into Caldrienne when the frontier route is open. An inland mountain line reaches Drossane, and a southern route reaches Miravelle. The alternative direct Karsenne–Calvernis alignment remains proposed, with no operational service. The atlas marks principal connections, not every local branch or settlement.

Serravonne to Auvrienne: approximately 350 km by rail, ordinarily 11–17 hours including normal stops and formalities.

Serravonne to Cressault crossing: approximately 575 km by rail, ordinarily 20–30 hours including normal stops and formalities.

Serravonne to Valdrec: approximately 805 km by rail, ordinarily 30–45 hours including normal stops and formalities.

Serravonne to Drossane: approximately 580 km by mountain rail, ordinarily 28–45 hours including normal stops and formalities.

Serravonne to Miravelle: approximately 475 km by rail, ordinarily 17–26 hours including normal stops and formalities.

Serravonne to Dalmor: approximately 270 km by sea, ordinarily 12–21 hours including normal stops and formalities.

These are practical passage estimates, not guaranteed schedules. Slow mountain running, border delays, weather, infrastructure damage and hunter activity can lengthen or suspend travel. Route kilometres follow the marked alignments rather than straight-line separation.

The Istravel Cut conservatory is 6 km from Serravonne by the upland railway branch. The first maintenance-trolley journey took 23 minutes. This branch is too short to distinguish on the regional sheet.

Auvrienne — city record. Auvrienne, Veyrasse’s capital, rises in terraces above an extensive railway basin. Freight warehouses, cranes and furnace-lit workshops occupy the lower city. Retaining walls support roads climbing toward pale government buildings with steep roofs and narrow towers. Gun positions overlook the railway cutting. Electric trams serve the streets. Near the freight-yard exit stand a booking office and a glass-covered street plan; farther uphill are an iron-railed monument and an illuminated inn. A bookseller occupies a nearer shopfront.

The Auvrienne Collegium of Civil Engineering occupies a broad terrace behind iron railings, with a grey-stone main building, courtyard and teaching workshops. Odran Savel serves as Examiner in Mechanics and sponsors Galahad’s work. Following completion of all curricula, Galahad remains a resident scholar and occasional teacher, receiving a stipend alongside lodging and meals. The library has been read twice; specialised collections and laboratories retain separate access arrangements. Institutional and professional connections support his expanding research.

The Margrave resides and governs in a fortified palace and government precinct on Auvrienne’s upper terraces, overlooking the city and railway basin. The household occupies the palace; adjoining buildings contain the chancery, treasury and military secretariat. Court and state policy are centred there, while municipal offices administer the city. The Collegium maintains connections through engineering work and patronage.

Odran Savel lives at 37 Rue Cendravel, upstairs over a bookbinder’s shop. A side door with a brass bell opens onto the stairwell. The address lies about ten minutes on foot from the Collegium gate.

Vordrake — furnace drake. The Vordrake, also called the furnace drake, is a house-sized winged reptile capable of breathing flame. Folded wings lie along its flanks in overlapping seams; ridged throat folds hang below a wedge-shaped head, with pale mineral growths along the jaw. Its exceptionally dense white cranial bone is known from natural histories and prized for rare weapons. Hunting accounts describe organised armed parties and substantial ammunition expenditure. Bringing one down barehanded lies beyond ordinary local expectations.

Veyrasse — family standing and currency. Noble houses stand above named common families; people without a recognised surname occupy the lowest social rank. Lineage influences access and official assumptions, even when institutional sponsorship permits an audience. Professional ability and patronage can win opportunities without conferring nobility. A stated family connection and completed legal registration are distinct matters. Veyrasse accounts use the lorrat, divided into one hundred brins. A skilled worker may earn roughly twenty-five lorrats a month.

The chancery occupies the eastern approach to the palace, joined to neighbouring offices by a roofed gallery. Bronze grilles conceal drainage outlets; carved stonework integrates with the hillside’s supporting structures. Portraits, lineage plaques and dark green leather chairs furnish its waiting gallery. Cyrrel Vaust serves as Deputy assessor for works expenditure, examining public-works claims and arranging defined technical commissions.

Southern pumping works. Ottrel Cevrane has worked with Galahad on budgeted material and flow improvements implemented in stages. Operating returns show lower vibration, steadier delivery and fewer interruptions in the altered sections. The installation supplies an uphill main and upper service reservoir. Discrepancies in delivery and pumping effort beyond the improved sections are now the subject of Galahad’s commissioned examination. The pump house and reservoir use differing daily reporting cutoffs; the full cause remains unresolved.

Iseva Dorlac sells carved ornaments and small luxury goods in Auvrienne. Her shop presents individual pieces against dark cloth beneath glass. She sells Galahad’s traditional charms with maker attribution and retains one quarter of each retail receipt.

Valesse Orchant teaches the older arts privately in Auvrienne. Her working room contains hanging cords, narrow cabinets and brushes. Her instruction examines attention, association, repetition and the relation between sign, material and intended purpose. Galahad’s experiments with her have produced impressions that linger in some charms for hours; dependable protection has not been demonstrated.

Veyrasse — noble grants and households. Women and men may head noble houses, hold property and inherit rank on equal terms under the governing grant. Lineage, wealth, service and patronage remain decisive distinctions. The Margrave may create minor hereditary noble houses by formal grant within the charter. The recognised branch and succession are specified; land, military privileges and political seats require separate provision. Buying an estate does not itself confer nobility.

Recognised parents included in a founding noble grant may receive matching familial titles, Mother of the House and Father of the House. The titles honour their relationship to the house head, independently of their relative participation in raising that person. In the intended Orsival grant their styles would be Lady Corva Orsival and Sir Veskan Orsival. Household responsibilities and delegated authority are assigned separately. Neither familial title confers regency, co-rule or guardianship over the head’s decisions. The proposed grant has not yet been obtained.

Planetary population survey. Malaspina supports approximately 1.21 billion people. Regional estimates total 1,209.2 million: Otranto 757.0 million, Vesalius 340.4 million and Morholt 111.8 million. Registers are uneven, borders disputed and wilderness settlements difficult to count. These figures describe inhabitants rather than mobilisable armies. The five eastern Vesalian states together account for 68.6 million people under separate governments. Veyrasse's 15.7 million occupy a claimed area of roughly 237,000 square kilometres, with settlement concentrated in defended districts.

Otranto: crowns, republics and disputed authority. Veldrassen is an old composite monarchy whose provincial bargains constrain taxation and mobilisation. Its large industrial base supports foundries, railways, arsenals and diversified manufacturing. Ostrevain is a centralising monarchy extending tighter administration across an extensive agricultural hinterland and expanding modern arsenals. Their governments command substantial resources but must bargain with institutions within their own territories.

Rovessara is a coastal commercial republic with strong precision, electrical, optical and aircraft-engine industries alongside a diversified economy. Its financiers and merchants hold interests overseas. Brannervaux is a river federation of unequal cities and estates, negotiating water allocation and taxation; agricultural processing, chemistry and major waterworks sustain its economy. Cervaud is a militarised border duchy under competing larger patrons' influence. Veylac is a smaller industrial republic with unresolved frontier disputes.

Ossavren's former crownlands contain rival claimants, provincial armies and ports administering separate customs. Veldrassen and Ostrevain support different contenders. The old crown's population and industry remain divided among authorities; no single palace commands them all. Smaller states, clients and autonomous territories fill the remaining political landscape. Annexation, foreign concessions and limited sovereignty are established realities.

Morholt: valleys, concessions and fortress jurisdictions. Rovengard is the largest single monarchy, centred on settled southern valleys with scattered forest and mountain strongholds. Varnesk is a mining and industrial league in which councils and foundry interests negotiate control; specialist steels, bearings and durable machinery are important trades. Galdresk's wardenship combines chartered orders, estates and civilian institutions, with expertise in field medicine and communications and small houses preserving the older arts. Halskert is a river republic whose seasonal shipping and agricultural valleys sustain influential dock and mill proprietors.

Beyond these governments lie numerous fortress jurisdictions, dependent districts and settlements. Some mineral and railway concessions are financed by Otrantan interests while local authorities retain civil government. Food, heating and seasonal transport constrain military operations. Great forest claims encompass little dependable tax revenue or manpower; control follows defended valleys and supply routes.

Vesalius beyond the eastern chart. Tervayne is a western maritime power separated from Veyrasse by roughly two thousand kilometres of uplands, forests and intervening jurisdictions. There is no continuous transcontinental railway. Its shipping interests compete with Calvernis overseas; its army is not stationed at Veyrasse's frontier.

Vardol lies farther north beyond Caldrienne's northern approaches. It rivals the inland realm of Averholt, whose populated basins and provincial arrangements shape its government. Their contested frontier and internal obligations consume resources that cannot simply be directed toward annexing the eastern coast.

Serevask's disputed federation collectively contains 58.4 million inhabitants, but the federal seat effectively administers only 13 million. Varnelle's delta authorities control commercial customs and their own troops; Kelbrun's upriver councils and plantation interests maintain separate levies; Gavrel's chartered march houses retain armed forces. Disputes over debt, water and federal authority have produced recurring internal conflict. Southern workshops preserve experience in rubber chemistry, filtration and medicine across these divided jurisdictions.

Elsewhere stand smaller states, independent ports and commercial territories. Veyrasse's security depends on its own army and revenues, difficult inland approaches, conditional partnerships and other powers' competing interests. Karsenne guards its passes; Calvernis resists a single power monopolising coastal commerce; Ceralte's maritime partnerships matter. Rivalries remain real, coalitions uncertain and defeat possible. Hunter attacks burden all governments without guaranteeing any border.

Industry and the circulation of knowledge. Industrial capability varies between districts as well as countries. The leading centres possess mature steelworking, aluminium production, casting, welding, machine tools, electrical networks, industrial chemistry and combustion engines. Conventional land armies, propeller aircraft and steam or diesel shipping depend on fuel, skilled labour and reliable maintenance. Experimental radio detection remains a developing field. Older machinery continues in widespread service alongside the most modern local equipment.

Regional concentrations of expertise arise from institutions, resources, trade and accumulated practice. Large states possess diversified economies; a famous precision workshop does not make its country the sole source of precision work. New designs may exceed current practice, while reproducible manufacture and large-scale adoption present their own demands.

Institutions of the older arts. Reliable practitioners are exceptionally rare, but accumulated records are much more extensive. Historians, physicians, scribes and instrument makers sustain schools whose few gifted members may travel between patrons. A teaching house can preserve generations of observations without producing an exceptional pupil in every generation.

Veldrassen maintains court examination offices and provincial registries. Rovessaran institutes and hospitals collect documented cases; Brannervaux's estates preserve private archives. Small teaching houses accompany Galdresk's wardens, while guarded Varnesk workshops occasionally collaborate with practitioners. Ceralte has maritime traditions, and Vesalian ports carry itinerant teachers and texts alongside private circles such as those in Auvrienne.

Scholarly, hereditary and religious schools dispute method and interpretation within each society. Divination, warding, telekinesis, ritual binding and rare experiments with machinery remain living pursuits. Ordinary study can preserve and interpret knowledge without granting every student the ability to perform it. The Collegium's limited regard for these subjects is a local academic attitude. Orchant's instruction and Galahad's observed lingering charm impressions remain part of this wider tradition; dependable protective effects remain unproven.

Residents of concessions and overseas interests are counted by their geographic location, once only.

Planetary survey IV. The continuous atlas follows continental shores into the Eastern Marches without a separate chart frame. Surveyed Eastern Marches locations and railway distances remain those of the regional record. The district register records 887 settlements across the three continents. Trunk and branch railways, district roads and shipping corridors connect fortified markets, industrial towns, administrative centres and ports. Rivers, tributaries, wooded country and mountain belts complete the closer survey; smaller villages and approach tracks remain uncharted. Cross-border services depend on agreements and conditions. No continuous railway connects Tervayne to eastern Veyrasse.

Serevask’s federal seat and the authorities of Varnelle, Kelbrun and Gavrel retain their separate jurisdictions.
